reminder: A cyclic subgroup is the set of all integer powers of one [element](c:element) of a [group](c:group).
definition: For an [element](c:element) $g$ of a [group](c:group) $G$, the cyclic subgroup generated by $g$ is $\langle g\rangle=\{g^n : n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. It is the smallest [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $G$ that contains $g$. It is a [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group), and its size is the [order](c:order-of-an-element) of $g$ when that order is finite.
examples: In $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ the subgroup $\langle 3\rangle=3\mathbb{Z}$ is cyclic and infinite.
In $S_3$ the 3-cycle $(1\,2\,3)$ generates $\{e,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$, a cyclic subgroup of order 3.
Non-example: The Klein four-group $\{e,a,b,ab\}$ is not a cyclic subgroup of itself, because no single element generates all four elements.

steps: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group) and $g$ an [element](c:element) of $G$.
The set $\langle g\rangle$ contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses.
So $\langle g\rangle$ is a subgroup of $G$, and the added condition is that one element generates it.
links.why: It shows that a cyclic subgroup is the simplest subgroup to build, so many questions about it reduce to one element.

reminder: A cylindrical measure is a finitely additive measure on cylinder sets whose finite-dimensional images are genuine probability measures.
definition: Let $E$ be a [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) with [dual space](c:dual-space) $E'$. A cylinder set is a set $\{x\in E:(\ell_1(x),\dots,\ell_n(x))\in B\}$ with $\ell_i\in E'$ and $B$ a [Borel set](c:borel-set) of $\mathbb{R}^n$. A cylindrical (probability) measure is a finitely additive function $\mu$ on the cylinder sets with $\mu(E)=1$ such that, for all $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n$, the map $B\mapsto\mu(\{x:(\ell_i(x))_i\in B\})$ is a countably additive [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
examples: The standard Gaussian cylindrical measure on an infinite-dimensional [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) has a standard normal law on every finite-dimensional projection.
Every Borel probability measure on $E$ restricts to a cylindrical measure on $E$.
Non-example: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$, restricted to cylinder sets of $E=\mathbb{R}$, has infinite total mass, so it is not a cylindrical probability measure.

steps: Take a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $E$.
Every cylinder set is a Borel set, because each functional in the dual space is continuous.
Restrict $\mu$ to the cylinder sets; the restriction is finitely additive with total mass 1.
Each image under $(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_n)$ is a push-forward of $\mu$, hence a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
links.why: It shows that Borel probability measures sit inside cylindrical measures, and the Gaussian example shows the inclusion is strict.

reminder: A definite form looks like one fixed model covector in a suitable basis of each tangent space.
definition: Fix a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ of dimension $n$ and a $p$-covector $\phi\in\wedge^pV^*$. A [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ of degree $p$ on an $n$-dimensional [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $X$ is definite on $\phi$ when, for every $x\in X$, some linear isomorphism $T_xX\to V$ carries $\omega_x$ to $\phi$. Equivalently, $\omega_x$ lies in the [orbit](c:orbit) of $\phi$ under the [general linear group](c:general-linear-group) of $V$.
examples: A [volume form](c:volume-form) on an $n$-manifold is definite on $dx^1\wedge\dots\wedge dx^n$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
A [symplectic form](c:symplectic-form) on a $2n$-manifold is definite on $\sum_i dx^i\wedge dy^i$ of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$.
A 3-form on a 7-manifold that is pointwise the [associative 3-form](c:associative-3-form) of $\mathbb{R}^7$ is definite.
Non-example: A 2-form on a 3-manifold that vanishes at some points and not at others is not definite, because the zero covector and a nonzero covector lie in different orbits.

steps: Start with a [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ of degree $p$ on a smooth manifold $X$.
Fix a model covector $\phi$ on a vector space $V$ of dimension $\dim X$.
Require that each value $\omega_x$ corresponds to $\phi$ under some identification of $T_xX$ with $V$.
The frames that realize this correspondence form a [G-structure](c:g-structure) whose group is the stabilizer of $\phi$.
links.why: It shows that a definite form is a differential form that carries a geometric structure, namely a G-structure.

steps: Take a [symplectic form](c:symplectic-form) $\omega$ on a manifold of dimension $2n$.
At each point $\omega_x$ is nondegenerate, so $T_xX$ has a symplectic basis.
In that basis $\omega_x=\sum_i dx^i\wedge dy^i$, which is the fixed model covector.
So $\omega$ is definite on this model, and closedness is an extra condition that a definite form need not have.
links.why: It shows that symplectic geometry is the closed case of one definite-form pattern.

steps: Take a [volume form](c:volume-form) $\omega$, a nowhere-zero $n$-form on an $n$-manifold.
At each point $\omega_x$ is a nonzero element of the line $\wedge^nT_x^*X$.
A linear map with the right determinant carries $\omega_x$ to $dx^1\wedge\dots\wedge dx^n$.
So $\omega$ is definite on this standard $n$-form.
links.why: It shows that a volume form is the simplest definite form, and the same pattern then applies to higher degrees.

reminder: A subspace $A$ of $X$ is a deformation retract when a homotopy shrinks $X$ onto $A$.
definition: Let $i:A\to X$ be the inclusion of a subspace of a [topological space](c:topological-space). The subspace $A$ is a deformation retract when there is a [retraction](c:retract) $r:X\to A$ with $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_A$ and a [homotopy](c:homotopy) from $i\circ r$ to $\mathrm{id}_X$. If this homotopy is constant on $A$, the retract is called strong.
examples: The circle $S^1$ is a deformation retract of $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\}$ by $H(x,t)=(1-t)x+t\,x/|x|$.
The origin is a deformation retract of $\mathbb{R}^n$ by $H(x,t)=(1-t)x$.
Non-example: A point of the circle $S^1$ is a retract of $S^1$ through the constant map, but not a deformation retract, because $S^1$ is not homotopy equivalent to a point.

steps: Let $i:A\to X$ be the inclusion and $r:X\to A$ the retraction.
Then $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_A$ holds exactly, with no homotopy needed.
The deformation gives a homotopy $i\circ r\simeq\mathrm{id}_X$.
So $i$ is a [homotopy equivalence](c:homotopy-equivalence) with inverse $r$, and the added condition is that one of the two homotopies is an identity.
links.why: It shows that a deformation retract has the same homotopy type as the big space, so invariants of $X$ can be computed on $A$.

steps: A [retract](c:retract) has a retraction $r$ with $r\circ i=\mathrm{id}_A$.
A deformation retract keeps this retraction.
It adds a homotopy from $i\circ r$ to $\mathrm{id}_X$.
links.why: It shows exactly what a retract needs to become a deformation retract: the composite $i\circ r$ must be homotopic to the identity.

reminder: The degree of a nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) is the largest exponent of $x$ with a nonzero coefficient.
definition: For a nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p=a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the degree is the largest [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ with $a_n\neq 0$. The zero polynomial has no degree in $\mathbb{N}$; by convention it gets degree $-\infty$. The degree is defined for elements of the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[x]$.
examples: A nonzero constant such as $7$ has degree $0$.
Over a domain, degrees add under products: $\deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g$.
Non-example: The zero polynomial has no largest exponent with a nonzero coefficient, so it has no degree in $\mathbb{N}$.

steps: A one-variable polynomial is a polynomial in the single variable $x$.
Each monomial $a_ix^i$ has total degree $i$.
The total degree of $p$ is the largest $i$ with $a_i\neq 0$.
This largest $i$ is exactly the degree of $p$.
links.why: It shows that the usual degree is the one-variable case of total degree.

reminder: Dehn surgery removes a solid torus around a knot from a [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) and glues a solid torus back differently.
definition: Let $K$ be a [knot](c:knot) in a [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) $M$, with a [tubular neighborhood](c:tubular-neighborhood) $N\cong S^1\times D^2$, a [solid torus](c:solid-torus). Choose a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $\varphi$ from the boundary torus of $S^1\times D^2$ to the boundary torus of the exterior $M\setminus\mathrm{int}\,N$. The Dehn surgery is the manifold $(M\setminus\mathrm{int}\,N)\cup_\varphi(S^1\times D^2)$, and up to homeomorphism it depends only on the slope $p/q$ of the curve $\varphi$ gives to the meridian of the new solid torus.
examples: Surgery on the unknot in $S^3$ with slope $1/n$ gives $S^3$ again, and slope $0$ gives $S^2\times S^1$.
Surgery with slope $-1$ on the left-handed trefoil in $S^3$ gives the Poincaré homology sphere, up to orientation.
Non-example: A connected sum of two 3-manifolds removes balls, not solid tori around knots, so it is not a Dehn surgery.

steps: In dimension $n$, surgery on an embedded sphere $S^k\subset M$ removes a neighborhood $S^k\times D^{n-k}$.
It glues in $D^{k+1}\times S^{n-k-1}$ along the common boundary $S^k\times S^{n-k-1}$.
Take $n=3$ and $k=1$, with the circle $S^1$ a knot $K$.
Then the removed piece is a solid torus $S^1\times D^2$, and the glued piece is a solid torus $D^2\times S^1$.
links.why: It shows that Dehn surgery is the one-dimensional case of surgery in a 3-manifold, so general surgery tools apply to knots.

reminder: A full subcategory is dense when each object is the canonical [colimit](c:colimit) of the subcategory objects mapping into it.
definition: A [full subcategory](c:full-subcategory) $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ with inclusion $\iota$ is dense when the functor from $\mathcal{C}$ to [presheaves](c:presheaf) on $\mathcal{A}$ that sends $c$ to $\mathcal{C}(\iota-,c)$ is [fully faithful](c:fully-faithful). Equivalently, every object $c$ of $\mathcal{C}$ is the [colimit](c:colimit) of the objects of $\mathcal{A}$ over all maps into $c$.
examples: The one-object full subcategory on a singleton is dense in $\mathbf{Set}$, because each set is the colimit of its points.
The simplex category $\Delta$ is dense in $\mathbf{Cat}$, because the nerve functor is fully faithful.
Non-example: In $\mathbf{Ab}$, the full subcategory on $\mathbb{Z}$ is not dense, because maps that commute with multiplication by integers need not be additive.

steps: Let $\iota:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}$ be the inclusion of a [full subcategory](c:full-subcategory).
The inclusion is a functor, so the definition of a dense functor applies to it.
A functor is dense when its nerve functor into presheaves on $\mathcal{A}$ is fully faithful.
A dense subcategory is a full subcategory whose inclusion is a dense functor.
links.why: It shows that a dense subcategory is the case of a dense functor that is an inclusion, so results on dense functors apply.

reminder: A density operator is a positive self-adjoint operator of trace one on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
definition: A density operator on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is a [positive operator](c:positive-operator) $\rho$ that is [self-adjoint](c:self-adjoint-operator) and [trace-class](c:trace-class-operator) with $\mathrm{tr}\,\rho=1$. It describes the state of a quantum system. It is pure when $\rho^2=\rho$ and mixed otherwise.
examples: For a [unit vector](c:unit-vector) $\psi$, the projection $|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ is a pure density operator.
On $\mathbb{C}^n$ the maximally mixed state $\tfrac1n I$ is a density operator.
A probability vector $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ gives the diagonal density operator $\mathrm{diag}(p_1,\dots,p_n)$.
Non-example: The identity operator on $\mathbb{C}^2$ is positive and self-adjoint, but its trace is 2, so it is not a density operator.

steps: Take a density matrix $\rho$, a positive Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix with trace 1.
View $\rho$ as an operator on the Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^n$.
On a finite-dimensional space every operator is trace-class, so the trace condition is the only one left.
So $\rho$ is a density operator.
links.why: It shows that density operators extend density matrices to infinite-dimensional systems, where the trace-class condition matters.

reminder: In a dependency graph, each event is mutually independent of all events that are not its neighbors.
definition: Let $A_1,\dots,A_n$ be events for a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\Pr$. A dependency graph for them is a [graph](c:graph) on the [vertices](c:vertex) $1,\dots,n$ such that each $A_i$ is mutually [independent](c:independence) of the family $\{A_j : j\neq i,\ j \text{ not adjacent to } i\}$. This means that $\Pr[A_i\mid B]=\Pr[A_i]$ for every event $B$ built from those $A_j$ by complements and intersections with $\Pr[B]>0$, a [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) statement.
examples: If each $A_i$ depends only on a set $S_i$ of independent random variables, join $i$ and $j$ when $S_i\cap S_j\neq\emptyset$; this graph is a dependency graph.
Mutually independent events have the empty graph as a dependency graph.
The complete graph is always a dependency graph, but it carries no information.
Non-example: For independent fair bits $X,Y$, let $A=\{X=1\}$, $B=\{Y=1\}$ and $C=\{X=Y\}$. The empty graph is not a dependency graph, because $\Pr[C\mid A\cap B]=1$ differs from $\Pr[C]=\tfrac12$.

reminder: The depth of a finitely generated [module](c:module) is the length of any maximal [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) on it.
definition: Let $R$ be a [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring), $I$ an [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$ and $M$ a [finitely generated module](c:finitely-generated-module) with $IM\neq M$. The depth of $M$ along $I$ is the length of a longest [regular sequence](c:regular-sequence) on $M$ with entries in $I$, and all maximal such sequences have the same length. For a [local ring](c:local-ring) with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$, the depth of $M$ means its depth along $\mathfrak{m}$.
examples: For the local ring $R=k[x,y]_{(x,y)}$ the sequence $x,y$ is regular, so $\operatorname{depth}R=2$.
The residue field $k=R/\mathfrak{m}$ has depth $0$, because every element of $\mathfrak{m}$ kills $k$.
Non-example: In $k[x,y]$ the sequence $x,x$ is not regular, because $x$ is a zero divisor on $k[x,y]/(x)$, so the second $x$ adds nothing to the depth.

reminder: In detailed balance, the probability flow from state $i$ to state $j$ equals the flow from $j$ to $i$.
definition: Let $P=(p_{ij})$ be the transition matrix of a [Markov chain](c:markov-chain) on a countable state space, and let $\pi$ be a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on the states. The chain is in detailed balance with $\pi$ when $\pi_i\,p_{ij}=\pi_j\,p_{ji}$ for all states $i,j$. Then $\pi$ is stationary, so a chain started from $\pi$ is a [stationary process](c:stationary-process) that looks the same when time runs backward.
examples: A random walk on a finite connected graph that moves to a uniform random neighbor is in detailed balance with $\pi_v\propto\deg v$.
Every two-state chain with $p_{12},p_{21}>0$ is in detailed balance with its stationary distribution.

Non-example: A chain that moves $1\to2\to3\to1$ with probability 1 has the uniform stationary distribution but no detailed balance, because the flow from 1 to 2 is positive and the flow from 2 to 1 is zero.

reminder: The diagram of a structure $M$ lists all atomic and negated atomic facts about the elements of $M$.
definition: Let $M$ be a [first-order structure](c:structure) and let $L(M)$ be its language with a new constant $c_m$ for each element $m$ of $M$. The diagram of $M$ is the set of all atomic and negated atomic [sentences](c:first-order-sentence) of $L(M)$ that are true in $M$, and the elementary diagram is the set of all $L(M)$-sentences true in $M$. An $L(M)$-structure $N$ models the diagram exactly when $m\mapsto c_m^N$ is an [embedding](c:embedding) of $M$ into $N$, and it models the elementary diagram exactly when this map is an [elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding).
examples: For $M=(\mathbb{N},<)$ the diagram contains $c_2<c_5$, $\neg(c_5<c_2)$ and $c_3\neq c_4$.
For $M=(\mathbb{Z},+)$ the diagram contains $c_2+c_3=c_5$, so every model of it holds a copy of $\mathbb{Z}$ with its addition.
The elementary diagram of $(\mathbb{Q},<)$ also contains $\exists x\,(c_0<x\wedge x<c_1)$, which the plain diagram does not.
Non-example: The set of all true sentences of $M$ without constants is the theory of $M$, not its diagram, because it gives no names to the elements of $M$.

reminder: The function is differentiable at every point of the set and continuous on the closure of the set.
definition: A function $f$ between normed spaces satisfies this condition on a set $s$ when $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) on $s$ and the restriction of $f$ to the [closure](c:closure) of $s$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function). It is the hypothesis of boundary results such as the maximum modulus principle, where $f$ may fail to be differentiable on the boundary of $s$.
examples: Every differentiable function on the whole space, such as a polynomial, satisfies the condition on every set.
The function $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ on $s=(0,1)$ is differentiable on $s$ and continuous on $[0,1]$, although it is not differentiable at $0$.
Non-example: The function $f(x)=1/x$ on $s=(0,1)$ is differentiable on $s$, but it is unbounded near $0$, so it is not continuous on the closure $[0,1]$.

reminder: A differential graded algebra is a graded algebra with a degree one differential that squares to zero and obeys the Leibniz rule.
definition: A differential graded algebra over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $k$ is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) that is a [graded algebra](c:graded-algebra) $A=\bigoplus_nA^n$, together with a $k$-linear map $d:A^n\to A^{n+1}$ such that $d\circ d=0$ and $d(ab)=d(a)\,b+(-1)^{|a|}a\,d(b)$ for homogeneous $a,b$. So $(A,d)$ is a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) whose product is compatible with $d$.
examples: The de Rham complex $\Omega^\bullet(M)$ of a smooth manifold, with the wedge product and the exterior derivative.
Any associative algebra $A$, placed in degree $0$ with $d=0$.
The singular cochains of a space, with the cup product and the coboundary.
Non-example: Differentiation $f\mapsto f'$ on $k[x]$ with $x$ in degree $0$ obeys the Leibniz rule, but it does not raise degree and $d\circ d\neq0$, so it is not a differential.

steps: Start with a [graded algebra](c:graded-algebra) $A=\bigoplus_nA^n$.
Add a linear map $d$ that raises degree by one.
Require $d\circ d=0$, so that $A$ becomes a cochain complex.
Require the Leibniz rule $d(ab)=d(a)\,b+(-1)^{|a|}a\,d(b)$, so that the product and $d$ fit together.
links.why: It shows exactly what a differential graded algebra adds to a graded algebra: a differential that is a graded derivation.

steps: Take the [de Rham complex](c:de-rham-complex) $\Omega^\bullet(M)$ of a smooth manifold $M$.
Differential forms form a graded algebra under the wedge product.
The exterior derivative has degree one and squares to zero.
It obeys $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{|\alpha|}\alpha\wedge d\beta$, so $\Omega^\bullet(M)$ is a differential graded algebra.
links.why: It shows that the de Rham complex is the basic example from geometry, and the definition abstracts its algebraic structure.

reminder: A differential inequality compares the derivative of a function with an expression in the function, such as $u'\le\beta u$.
definition: A differential inequality for an unknown function $u$ is an inequality such as $u'(t)\le F(t,u(t))$ that relates $t$, the values of $u$ and the [derivatives](c:derivative) of $u$. A [differentiable function](c:differentiable-function) $u$ solves it on an interval $I$ when the inequality holds for every $t\in I$. Its solutions give bounds on $u$ instead of exact values.
examples: The inequality $u'\le\beta u$ on $[a,b]$ gives $u(t)\le u(a)\exp\!\big(\int_a^t\beta\big)$ by Grönwall's lemma.
The inequality $u'(t)\ge0$ on an interval says that $u$ is nondecreasing.
The inequality $|u'(t)|\le1$ says that $u$ is 1-Lipschitz.
Non-example: The condition $u(t)\le1$ for all $t$ is an inequality but not a differential inequality, because it does not involve a derivative of $u$.

steps: Take an [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $u'=F(t,u)$.
Replace the equals sign by $\le$ to get the differential inequality $u'\le F(t,u)$.
Every solution of the equation satisfies the inequality.
The inequality can have more solutions, so it gives bounds instead of exact values.
links.why: It shows that an equation is the boundary case of two inequalities, and that comparison arguments replace exact solving.

reminder: The digit sum of a natural number is the sum of the digits in its decimal writing.
definition: For a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n=\sum_{i=0}^{k}d_i10^i$ with [decimal digits](c:decimal-numeral-representation-of-the-natural-numbers) $0\le d_i\le9$, the digit sum is $s(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}d_i$. The same definition works in any base $b\ge2$, with digits $0\le d_i<b$.
examples: Since $10\equiv1\pmod 9$, the digit sum satisfies $s(n)\equiv n\pmod 9$; for example $2026$ and $s(2026)=10$ both leave remainder $1$.
Non-example: The number $1000$ has four digits but digit sum $1$, so counting digits is not the same as adding them.

reminder: A Dirac operator is a first-order differential operator on spinors whose square is a Laplace-type operator.
definition:
Let $S	o X$ be a [spinor bundle](c:spinor-bundle) over a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $X$, with an action $c$ of the [Clifford algebra](c:clifford-algebra) of the cotangent spaces and a compatible [connection](c:connection) $
abla$. The Dirac operator is the composite $D=c\circ
abla$, locally $D=\sum_i e_i\cdot
abla_{e_i}$ for an orthonormal frame $e_i$. It is a first-order [differential operator](c:differential-operator) on sections of $S$ whose principal symbol is Clifford multiplication, so $D^2$ has the principal symbol of the Laplacian.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^n$ with spinors in $\mathbb{C}^N$, $D=\sum_i\gamma_i\partial_i$ with $\gamma_i\gamma_j+\gamma_j\gamma_i=-2\delta_{ij}$ satisfies $D^2=-\Delta$.
On a spin manifold the spin Dirac operator satisfies the Lichnerowicz formula $D^2=\nabla^*\nabla+\tfrac14\,\mathrm{scal}$.
Non-example: The Laplacian $-\Delta$ on functions has order two, so it is not a Dirac operator; it is the square of one.

steps: A [differential operator](c:differential-operator) maps sections of one bundle to sections of another.
Here both bundles are the spinor bundle $S$.
Choose the first-order operator $c\circ\nabla$, a connection followed by Clifford multiplication.
Its principal symbol is Clifford multiplication by the covector, so its square has the symbol of a Laplacian.
links.why: It shows that a Dirac operator is a first-order operator that acts as a square root of a Laplace-type operator.

reminder: A Dirichlet series is a series $\sum a_nn^{-s}$ with complex coefficients $a_n$ and a complex variable $s$.
definition: A Dirichlet series is a [series](c:series) $\sum_{n\ge1}a_n\,n^{-s}$ with complex coefficients $a_n$ indexed by the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) and a [complex number](c:complex-number) $s$. It converges on a right half-plane $\mathrm{Re}\,s>\sigma$, or everywhere, or nowhere.
examples: The Riemann zeta function $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$, with $a_n=1$, for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$.
A Dirichlet $L$-series $\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)\,n^{-s}$ for a Dirichlet character $\chi$.
The series $\sum_{n\ge1}\mu(n)\,n^{-s}=1/\zeta(s)$ for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$, with the Möbius function $\mu$.
Non-example: A power series $\sum a_nz^n$ is not a Dirichlet series, because the variable sits in the base and not in the exponent.

steps: Take the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function) $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$ for $\mathrm{Re}\,s>1$.
Read it as a Dirichlet series with $a_n=1$ for every $n$.
Other coefficient sequences $a_n$ give other Dirichlet series.
links.why: It shows that the zeta function is the Dirichlet series with all coefficients equal to 1, and that the series form a wider family.

reminder: A discrete group is a [topological group](c:topological-group) whose topology is discrete, so every point is an open set.
definition: A discrete group is a [topological group](c:topological-group) whose topology is the [discrete topology](c:discrete-topology), so every subset is open. A [subgroup](c:subgroup) $\Gamma$ of a topological group $G$ is a discrete subgroup when it is a discrete group in the subspace topology.
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ form a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$, because each integer has a neighborhood with no other integer.
The group $SL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is a discrete subgroup of $SL_n(\mathbb{R})$.
Non-example: The rationals $\mathbb{Q}$ form a subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$ that is not discrete, because every interval around $0$ holds other rationals.

steps: Let $G$ be any group.
Give $G$ the [discrete topology](c:discrete-topology), where every subset is open.
Multiplication and inversion are continuous, because every map out of a discrete space is continuous.
So $G$ is a topological group, and a discrete group is the case where the topology is discrete.
links.why: It shows that every abstract group is a discrete group, so group theory is the case with no topology.

reminder: A discrete valuation ring is a principal ideal domain that has exactly one nonzero maximal ideal.
definition: A discrete valuation ring is a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain) $R$ that has exactly one nonzero [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak{m}$. Equivalently, $R$ is a [local ring](c:local-ring) that is a principal ideal domain but not a field; then $\mathfrak{m}=(\pi)$ and each nonzero element is $u\pi^n$ with $u$ a unit and $n\ge0$.
examples: The localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ of the integers at a prime $p$, with $\mathfrak{m}=(p)$.
The formal power series ring $k[[t]]$ over a field $k$, with $\mathfrak{m}=(t)$.
The ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of $p$-adic integers, with $\mathfrak{m}=(p)$.
Non-example: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ form a principal ideal domain with infinitely many nonzero maximal ideals, and a field has none, so neither is a discrete valuation ring.

steps: Start with a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain) $R$, so every ideal is generated by one element.
Count the nonzero maximal ideals; a field has none and $\mathbb{Z}$ has infinitely many.
Require exactly one nonzero maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$.
Then $R$ is local with $\mathfrak{m}=(\pi)$, and $R$ is a discrete valuation ring.
links.why: It shows which extra condition makes a principal ideal domain so simple that every nonzero element is a unit times a power of one element.

steps: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring with nonzero maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$.
The zero ideal is not maximal, because $R$ is not a field.
So $\mathfrak{m}$ is the only maximal ideal, and $R$ is a [local ring](c:local-ring).
A local ring is a discrete valuation ring when it is also a principal ideal domain that is not a field.
links.why: It shows that a discrete valuation ring is a local ring with a very strong extra condition on its ideals.

reminder: Disjoint paths between two [vertices](c:vertex) share no vertex except their ends.
definition: Let $s$ and $t$ be [vertices](c:vertex) of a [graph](c:graph). The [paths](c:is-path) $P_1,\dots,P_k$ from $s$ to $t$ are disjoint when no two of them share a vertex other than $s$ and $t$. In the edge-disjoint version, no two paths share an [edge](c:edge).
examples: In a cycle $C_n$, any two vertices are joined by exactly two disjoint paths, the two arcs of the cycle.
In the complete graph $K_n$, two vertices $s,t$ are joined by $n-1$ disjoint paths: the edge $st$ and the paths $s\,v\,t$ for the other $n-2$ vertices $v$.
Non-example: The paths $s\,a\,t$ and $s\,a\,b\,t$ both pass through $a$, so they are not disjoint.

reminder: A dissipative operator $A$ satisfies $\|(\lambda-A)x\|\ge\lambda\|x\|$ for all $\lambda>0$ and all $x$ in its domain.
definition: Let $A:D(A)\to X$ be a linear operator, possibly [unbounded](c:unbounded-operator), on a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$. The operator $A$ is dissipative when $\|(\lambda I-A)x\|\ge\lambda\|x\|$ for all $x\in D(A)$ and all $\lambda>0$. On a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) this is equivalent to $\mathrm{Re}\,\langle Ax,x\rangle\le0$ for all $x\in D(A)$.
examples: On a Hilbert space, $A=-I$ is dissipative, because $\mathrm{Re}\,\langle -x,x\rangle=-\|x\|^2\le0$.
The Dirichlet Laplacian on $H^2(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)\subset L^2(\Omega)$ is dissipative, because $\langle\Delta u,u\rangle=-\|\nabla u\|^2\le0$.
Non-example: The identity $I$ on a nonzero Hilbert space is not dissipative, because $\langle Ix,x\rangle=\|x\|^2>0$.

reminder: Divide and conquer splits a problem into smaller copies of itself, solves them by recursion and combines the answers.
definition: Divide and conquer is a method to design an [algorithm](c:algorithm). It splits an instance of size $n$ into $a$ subinstances of size about $n/b$, solves each one by [recursion](c:recursion), and combines the answers with extra work $f(n)$. Its running time then obeys a [recurrence relation](c:recurrence-relation) of the form $T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)$.
examples: Merge sort splits a list into two halves, sorts both and merges them, so $T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)$.
Binary search keeps one half of a sorted list, so $T(n)=T(n/2)+O(1)$.
Karatsuba multiplication reduces one product of $n$-digit numbers to three products of about $n/2$ digits, so $T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n)$.
Non-example: Computing $n!$ by $n!=n\cdot(n-1)!$ removes one element and does not split the input into parts of size $n/b$, so it is not divide and conquer.

reminder: In a division algebra, the equations $ax=b$ and $xa=b$ have a unique solution whenever $a\neq0$.
definition: A division algebra over a [field](c:field) $k$ is a [nonassociative algebra](c:nonassociative-algebra) $A$, a vector space with a [bilinear](c:bilinear-map) product that need not be associative, such that for each nonzero $a\in A$ and each $b\in A$ the equations $ax=b$ and $xa=b$ each have a unique solution $x\in A$. For a finite-dimensional algebra this holds exactly when $A$ has no zero divisors.
examples: The fields $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ and the [quaternions](c:quaternion) $\mathbb{H}$ are division algebras over $\mathbb{R}$.
The [octonions](c:octonion) form a division algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ that is not associative.
Non-example: The matrix algebra $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ is not a division algebra, because $a=\mathrm{diag}(1,0)$ satisfies $ax=0$ for many $x$, so solutions are not unique.

steps: Take a [division ring](c:division-ring) $D$ and let $k$ be its center, a field.
Then $D$ is an associative algebra over $k$.
For $a\neq0$ the inverse $a^{-1}$ exists, so $ax=b$ has the unique solution $x=a^{-1}b$ and $xa=b$ has the unique solution $x=ba^{-1}$.
So $D$ is a division algebra over $k$.
links.why: It shows that division algebras include all division rings, and also nonassociative examples such as the octonions.

steps: A [nonassociative algebra](c:nonassociative-algebra) is a vector space with a bilinear product that need not be associative.
Add the condition that $ax=b$ and $xa=b$ have unique solutions for every $a\neq0$.
This condition is the only extra structure, and associativity is not required.
links.why: It shows that a division algebra is a nonassociative algebra with unique division, so it covers the octonions.

reminder: The Dolbeault operator $\bar\partial$ is the part of the exterior derivative that raises the antiholomorphic degree by one.
definition: On a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$, the [exterior derivative](c:exterior-derivative) of a [differential form](c:differential-form) of type $(p,q)$ splits as $d=\partial+\bar\partial$, with $\partial$ of type $(p+1,q)$ and $\bar\partial$ of type $(p,q+1)$. The Dolbeault operator is $\bar\partial:\Omega^{p,q}(X)\to\Omega^{p,q+1}(X)$; it satisfies $\bar\partial^2=0$, and a function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) exactly when $\bar\partial f=0$.
examples: On $\mathbb{C}$, $\bar\partial f=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\bar z}\,d\bar z$, so $f$ is holomorphic exactly when $\bar\partial f=0$.
On $\mathbb{C}^2$, $\bar\partial(\bar z_1 z_2)=z_2\,d\bar z_1$.
Non-example: The operator $\partial:\Omega^{p,q}\to\Omega^{p+1,q}$ is the other part of $d$; it raises the holomorphic degree, so it is not the Dolbeault operator.

steps: In local holomorphic coordinates, $\bar\partial$ differentiates the coefficients of a form only with respect to the $\bar z_k$.
So $\bar\partial$ is linear, and it differentiates each coefficient at most once.
Hence $\bar\partial$ is a first-order linear [differential operator](c:differential-operator) between bundles of forms.
links.why: It shows that the Dolbeault operator is an ordinary first-order operator, so symbol and ellipticity methods apply to it.

reminder: A double integral adds up the values of a function of two variables over a region of the plane.
definition: For a bounded region $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ and a [Riemann integrable](c:riemann-integral) function $f$ on $D$, the double integral $\iint_Df\,dA$ is the limit of the sums $\sum_kf(x_k,y_k)\,\Delta A_k$ over finer and finer partitions of $D$ into small rectangles of area $\Delta A_k$. For a continuous $f$ on a rectangle $[a,b]\times[c,d]$ it equals the [iterated integral](c:iterated-integral) $\int_a^b\!\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx$.
examples: With $f=1$, the double integral $\iint_D1\,dA$ is the area of $D$.
For $f\ge0$, the double integral $\iint_Df\,dA$ is the volume of the solid under the graph of $f$ over $D$.
Non-example: The integral of $1/(x^2+y^2)$ over the unit disc does not exist as a finite number, because in polar coordinates it equals $2\pi\int_0^1\frac{dr}{r}$, which diverges.

steps: Take the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$, which gives each rectangle its area.
Integrate $f$ over $D$ with respect to this measure.
For a Riemann integrable $f$, the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) has the same value as the double integral.
links.why: It shows that the double integral is the Lebesgue integral for area measure, so measure-theoretic theorems apply to it.

reminder: A doubly stochastic matrix has nonnegative entries, and every row and every column sums to 1.
definition: A doubly stochastic matrix is a square [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ of real numbers with $a_{ij}\ge0$, $\sum_ja_{ij}=1$ for each row $i$, and $\sum_ia_{ij}=1$ for each column $j$. Equivalently, $A$ is a [nonnegative matrix](c:nonnegative-matrix) with $A\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{1}^{T}A=\mathbf{1}^{T}$.
examples: Every [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix) is doubly stochastic.
The matrix $\tfrac1nJ$ with every entry equal to $\tfrac1n$ is doubly stochastic.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0.3&0.7\\0.7&0.3\end{pmatrix}$ is doubly stochastic.
Non-example: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has row sums $1$ but column sums $2$ and $0$, so it is only row stochastic.

steps: A [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix) has exactly one entry $1$ in each row and each column, and zeros elsewhere.
So all its entries are nonnegative.
Every row sum and every column sum equals $1$.
Hence every permutation matrix is doubly stochastic.
links.why: It shows that permutation matrices are the simplest doubly stochastic matrices, and by the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem every doubly stochastic matrix is a convex combination of them.

reminder: A down-set is a subset of a poset that contains every element below each of its members.
definition: In a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) $(P,\le)$, a [subset](c:subset) $D\subseteq P$ is a down-set when $x\in D$ and $y\le x$ imply $y\in D$. For $x\in P$, the principal down-set of $x$ is ${\downarrow}x=\{y\in P:y\le x\}$.
examples: In $(\mathbb{N},\le)$ the set $\{0,1,2,3\}$ and the whole set $\mathbb{N}$ are down-sets.
In the divisibility order on positive integers, the set of divisors of $12$ is the principal down-set of $12$.
In the power set of $\{1,2,3\}$ ordered by inclusion, every family of subsets that is closed under taking subsets is a down-set.
Non-example: In $(\mathbb{N},\le)$ the set $\{2,5\}$ is not a down-set, because $5$ is in it but $3\le5$ is not.

reminder: An object $X$ is dualizable when it has a dual $X^*$ with evaluation and coevaluation maps that satisfy the zigzag identities.
definition: In a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $\mathcal{C}$ with [unit object](c:unit-object) $1$, an object $X$ is dualizable when there are an object $X^*$ and maps $\mathrm{ev}:X^*\otimes X\to1$ and $\mathrm{coev}:1\to X\otimes X^*$, called [evaluation](c:evaluation-map) and [coevaluation](c:coevaluation-map), such that the composites $X\to X\otimes X^*\otimes X\to X$ and $X^*\to X^*\otimes X\otimes X^*\to X^*$ are identities, up to associators and unitors.
examples: In finite-dimensional vector spaces with $\otimes$, the dual space $V^*$ is a dual of $V$, and a vector space is dualizable exactly when it is finite-dimensional.
In a [compact closed category](c:compact-closed-category) every object is dualizable.
Non-example: An infinite-dimensional vector space $V$ is not dualizable, because the zigzag identity would write $\mathrm{id}_V$ as a finite sum $x\mapsto\sum_i\varphi_i(x)v_i$, a map of finite rank.

steps: Take an object $X$ that is [self-dual](c:self-dual-object), so $X$ is a dual of itself.
The self-duality gives an evaluation $X\otimes X\to1$ and a coevaluation $1\to X\otimes X$.
These maps satisfy the zigzag identities.
So $X$ is dualizable with $X^*=X$.
links.why: It shows that dualizability is the weaker condition: the dual may be another object, and self-duality is the case where the dual is the object itself.

reminder: A Dynkin diagram is a graph that records the angles and relative lengths of the simple roots of a root system.
definition: Let $R$ be a finite reduced [root system](c:is-root-system) with a set $\Delta$ of [simple roots](c:simple-root). The Dynkin diagram of $R$ is the [graph](c:graph) with one vertex for each $\alpha\in\Delta$ and, for $\alpha\neq\beta$, $\langle\alpha,\beta^\vee\rangle\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ edges between $\alpha$ and $\beta$, with an arrow towards the shorter root when the edge is multiple. It encodes the [Cartan matrix](c:is-finite-cartan), so it determines the root system, and with it the simple [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra), up to isomorphism.
examples: The diagram $A_n$ is a chain of $n$ vertices joined by single edges; it belongs to $\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}(\mathbb{C})$.
The diagram $G_2$ has two vertices joined by a triple edge with an arrow towards the short root.
The diagram $D_4$ has one central vertex joined to three other vertices.
Non-example: A triangle of three vertices joined by single edges is not the Dynkin diagram of a finite root system; it is an affine diagram.
